narration: Two teams of diggers started at opposite ends of a hill in Jerusalem and tried to meet in total darkness. This was not a legend. It was a water problem. Jerusalem's most reliable water source, the Gihon Spring, sat outside the city walls. In a siege, an enemy could control it, and the people inside could die of thirst. The Bible says King Hezekiah of Judah stopped the upper outlet of the Gihon and brought its water down to the west side of the City of David. Most scholars connect this work with the threat of an Assyrian invasion, although the exact date is still debated. The result was a tunnel cut through solid rock, about 533 meters long, carrying water from the spring to the Pool of Siloam inside the city. The route is not straight. It curves like a snake, and historians still argue about why. One idea is that the workers followed natural cracks in the rock. Here is the surprising part. In 1880, an inscription was discovered on the tunnel wall. It describes the final moments of the work: the two crews swinging their picks toward each other, hearing each other's voices through the rock, and finally breaking through, pick against pick. Then the water flowed. It is one of the oldest known Hebrew inscriptions of its kind. A short verse in the Bible, a curving tunnel and a few carved lines all point to the same story: a city racing to protect its water before the enemy arrived.
